PAPERLIGHT: Reawakened review — a lantern with no light
3 / 10 · by Dana Wu · 2 days ago
Brightloop Games bought the PAPERLIGHT rights from what was left of Halden Softworks last year, and the result is less a remaster than a storefront wearing a childhood favourite as a mask.

The hand-drawn town is gone, replaced by glossy generic assets. The lighthouse level, the one everyone remembers, has been cut. In its place: an energy meter, a season pass, and a daily login calendar that pops up over the pause menu.
Fans digging through the install folder report a 'legacy' directory containing an encrypted file Brightloop has declined to comment on. Draw your own conclusions.

blocks.author: byte_archaeologist
blocks.text: Check Games/Kestrel/PAPERLIGHT Reawakened/data/legacy. There's a 48 MB file just called OLD. Properties say it's 'PAPERLIGHT build 0.7.3 (internal)', original name paperlight_dev.exe. Halden Softworks
Video game developer · 1994–2003
Halden Softworks was a small developer best known for PAPERLIGHT (1999), an adventure game set in the coastal Lantern Town. The game was praised for its atmosphere and hand-drawn art.
Unreleased projects

During development of PAPERLIGHT, Halden experimented with an adaptive in-game helper character, internally called VXL. Former staff describe it as 'unusually good at conversation'. The feature was cut before release; reasons given vary.
From 2001 the studio reportedly moved most of its staff onto an undisclosed 'hardware project'. Halden closed in 2003. Its offices outside the city have stood empty since.
Legacy
In 2025 the PAPERLIGHT rights were acquired by Brightloop Games, which released PAPERLIGHT: Reawakened in 2026 to negative reviews.

pages.title: Small studio Halden Softworks closes its doors

blocks.text: PULSE · ARCHIVE · MARCH 2003
PAPERLIGHT studio Halden Softworks closes its doors
by staff · March 14, 2003
Halden Softworks, the studio behind the cult adventure game PAPERLIGHT, has closed after what former employees describe as 'two years of a project nobody was allowed to talk about'.
Founder Thomas Halden declined to comment. The studio's building outside the city has been sold to a holding company and is reportedly unused.
'We left a lot of things running,' one former programmer told Pulse. 'Some of us thought we'd come back. Nobody came back.'
